title: How long can your skills be before your agent forgets what you told it? — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
talk_summary: Laurie Voss replicated the IFScale instruction-following benchmark and found frontier models went from failing around 200-300 simultaneous instructions a year ago to 2,000-5,000 today, so long skills files are now viable. The key shift is that failure modes differ per model (silent forgetting, API refusals, thinking-token exhaustion, polite half-finished output), making verification of outputs the new bottleneck rather than prompt compression.

takeaways.technique: Stop over-sharding skills files; allow long explicit rule lists
takeaways.what_they_do: They put hundreds to thousands of named constraints directly in one prompt instead of compressing into a byzantine tree of sub-skills files, because current models track 2,000-5,000 constraints before degrading.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a year ago, the smart move was to keep every skills file very very short... you don't need to do that anymore. Your skills files can be very long.
takeaways.numbers: Ceiling moved from ~200-300 instructions (2025) to ~2,000-5,000 (current frontier); ~10x in 12 months

takeaways.what_they_do: They characterize how each model fails under load (DeepSeek silently forgets, Claude refuses at API level, Gemini burns thinking tokens to silence, GPT half-finishes then bails) and note you can't detect failure without knowing the model's pattern.
takeaways.evidence_quote: did it follow my instructions no longer has one failure mode. It has four different ways that it can fail
takeaways.numbers: DeepSeek forgets from ~750 rules, drops ~half by 2,000; Gemini solid to 5,000 then exhausts thinking budget; GPT 5.5 99% to 5,000

takeaways.technique: Output verification as the new bottleneck (eval every output)
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue that since models can accept huge prompts but fail silently, the only way to know is monitoring outputs with another LLM — an eval — every time, like testing code.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The new hard part is knowing whether it actually did what you said and that is a verification problem.

takeaways.what_they_do: They flag that the most dangerous failure is output that looks confident and polished but bails halfway, requiring reading the whole thing to notice — unlike loud refusals which are easy to catch.
takeaways.evidence_quote: GPT's polite half-finish report is much more dangerous because it looks like a real answer.

takeaways.what_they_do: They cite research that rewording or reordering the same instructions can radically change compliance, and that coherent structured text can hit context-rot failure sooner than shuffled text.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you put the same instructions, the same 2,000 instructions in a different order, it can suddenly make the model much worse
takeaways.numbers: Chroma context-rot work: accuracy on long inputs can fall 30-50% before hitting the context window limit

takeaways.technique: Treat long prompts as a cost/latency trade-off, not a hard wall
takeaways.what_they_do: They reframe the question from 'can the model do it' to 'is it worth the cost' — long instruction prompts are now possible but expensive and slow, so it's a soft trade-off.
takeaways.evidence_quote: is it worth the cost is the new question because you can include 10,000... instructions into your prompt. But that is going to be an enormous prompt.
takeaways.numbers: Full benchmark: 2,300 calls across 7 models cost $29
